title: First jobs: trio in a Gentilly barn and the Silver Star
summary: Herbert Moran urges him to keep drumming; the trio with Walter Nelson plays a barn job, then the Silver Star nightclub with hired sidemen.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Oh, that was around in the 1940s. Yeah, in the 1940s, because I was living across the street at the time, at 825 North Galvestre. And the first job that, after he found out that I was playing that good, Herbert Moran, one of our old time trumpet men, he was a wonderful jazz man on the trumpet. He left Chicago and came back home. And he heard me play. He said, Joe, he said, why don't you try to stick with the drums? I said, well, if I'm playing that good, I said, I don't mind sticking with it, but if I'm bad, I said, I'd much rather get out of it. So, the first job we got together was the three of us. It was him, Walter Nelson on the guitar, and myself on the drums. We played a job back in Gentilly, in a barn, a cow barn, a stall, you know. Okay, I was in one stall, he was in the other two stalls. Now, we had, now I had trouble trying to listen to what the heck they was playing, see. But, the acoustic in that place must have been mildly good, because the sound was coming over fine. Well, after that, Walter Nelson had got a job at the Silver Star nightclub at St. Pernod and St. Claude on the downtown in River Corner. It was run by Joe Cianelli. Well, we started playing there every Friday and Saturday. Well, we used to have a little difficulty in hiring musicians outside of Moraine and myself. We'd cut the job call for six men. Well, we used to hire George Lewis, we used to hire Slowdray. And we had a fellow on saxophone from uptown by the name of Albert. I never did know his full name, but I knew they called him Albert, but he was a darn good sax man. Well, we used to play there every weekend until one Saturday night he put in a flow show. Well, he didn't have no license for that. So, the Lord stepped in and took us all down. So, I had to pay a ten dollar fine. My wife paid a ten dollar fine to get me out. Well, I said, never no more of Joe Cianelli's Silver Star for me, if that's the way he's going to operate. So, in the meantime, we were bringing our jobs around town. George Lewis had got a job to play on that voidsman for a prizefighter back at the Pelican ballpark. So, when we got through playing at that voidsman, he said, Joe, he said, how about joining up with me? Well, that was after he had come back from New York. That was in 1945. I said, yeah, I said, I'll play with you until somebody better comes along. He said, all right, he said, you can play all jobs with me. Well, we started getting jobs out in the, uh, one of them Catholic schools out in town there. I forget the name of the school, but I can't think of it right now, anyhow. But anyway, I continued to play with him, and he told me, he said, Joe, I like the way you're playing. You're playing that old style drumming and that's what I want. He said, I'm going to keep this thing going. He said, now we done revived it in New York, and we're going to try to keep it going here. He said, it'll take a little time to build up, but he said, it'll come through. Well, sure enough, it did come through. We played at the Royal Room on Royal Street one night, or whatever, during the time of Tony Almericka's reign. He was, he used to play there all the time.
Yes. Would that be the Parisian Room?
